questions.prompt: A company announces a large all-stock acquisition and its own share price falls. What inference are investors most likely making?
choices: That the target is a poor business
That management believes its own shares are overvalued and is spending cheap currency
That the deal will certainly be blocked by regulators
That the company has run out of borrowing capacity and is therefore distressed
questions.explanation: Paying with shares you believe are undervalued is expensive, so choosing stock signals the opposite. It is a tendency rather than a law — size and leverage capacity also drive the choice.

questions.prompt: How does paying in stock rather than cash change who bears the risk of the deal failing to deliver?
choices: It removes the risk entirely through diversification
It transfers all risk to the target's shareholders
It shares the risk, because the target's shareholders now own part of the combined company
It has no effect on risk allocation, only on tax
questions.explanation: Cash lets the target's shareholders exit with certainty and concentrates the outcome on the buyer's shareholders. Stock makes them joint owners of whatever happens next.

questions.prompt: A founder is retiring and will not stay with the business. Which consideration is she most likely to prefer, and why might she still accept shares?
choices: Stock, because it defers her involvement
Cash for certainty — though a share exchange may defer her capital gains tax
An earn-out, because it maximises headline price
Cash, because share consideration is not permitted for founders
questions.explanation: A retiring seller wants certainty, so cash. But receiving cash often triggers an immediate capital gains charge, while a share-for-share exchange can defer it — which is why some sellers accept a lower headline price in stock.

questions.prompt: An earn-out makes part of the price depend on the target's performance after closing, and is a common source of later disputes.
questions.explanation: True. It bridges a disagreement about the forecast, but the buyer then controls the business whose performance determines what it must pay — which is exactly why they generate litigation.

questions.prompt: A buyer must choose between funding a large acquisition entirely in cash or entirely in stock. Set out the trade-off for its own shareholders, and explain what each choice communicates to the market.
rubric: States that cash concentrates both synergies and downside on the buyer's existing shareholders
States that stock dilutes them but transfers part of the risk to the target's shareholders
Explains the signalling logic: stock is attractive when management thinks its shares are expensive, cash when it thinks they are cheap
Notes practical constraints that may override signalling — deal size, existing leverage, credit rating, and tax treatment for the seller
Mentions that a stock deal's value moves with the share price before closing, and that collars exist to manage this
